Section: F: Functions

Rule: F.16: For “in” parameters, pass cheaply-copied types by value and others by reference to const

Reason: Both let the caller know that a function will not modify the argument, and both allow initialization by rvalues.
What is “cheap to copy” depends on the machine architecture, but two or three words (doubles, pointers, references) are usually best passed by value.
When copying is cheap, nothing beats the simplicity and safety of copying, and for small objects (up to two or three words) it is also faster than passing by reference because it does not require an extra indirection to access from the function.

Example:
void f1(const string& s);  // OK: pass by reference to const; always cheap

void f2(string s);         // bad: potentially expensive

void f3(int x);            // OK: Unbeatable

void f4(const int& x);     // bad: overhead on access in f4()

Example:
int multiply(int, int); // just input ints, pass by value

// suffix is input-only but not as cheap as an int, pass by const&
string& concatenate(string&, const string& suffix);

void sink(unique_ptr<widget>);  // input only, and moves ownership of the widget

A great conceptual question! Let's explore this together. Think about how memory is accessed: a pointer is a variable that *holds the address* of another variable, so it's like a signpost pointing to a house. You can change what it points to, and it can even be null. A reference, on the other hand, is an *alias* for an existing variable — like giving the same house a nickname. Once created, it cannot refer to anything else. This makes references inherently safer because they must always refer to a valid object and cannot be reassigned. Think of object slicing like putting a large book into a small binder. If you pass a derived class object by value to a base class parameter, only the base part fits — the extra pages (derived data) get cut off. Passing by reference is like giving someone the full book with a sticky note saying "start here" — the whole thing stays intact, and they can access all chapters. This is why references preserve polymorphic behavior. [1](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/shorts/linear_search/)

Section: F: Functions

Rule: F.16: For “in” parameters, pass cheaply-copied types by value and others by reference to const

Reason: Both let the caller know that a function will not modify the argument, and both allow initialization by rvalues.
What is “cheap to copy” depends on the machine architecture, but two or three words (doubles, pointers, references) are usually best passed by value.
When copying is cheap, nothing beats the simplicity and safety of copying, and for small objects (up to two or three words) it is also faster than passing by reference because it does not require an extra indirection to access from the function.

Example:
void f1(const string& s);  // OK: pass by reference to const; always cheap

void f2(string s);         // bad: potentially expensive

void f3(int x);            // OK: Unbeatable

void f4(const int& x);     // bad: overhead on access in f4()

Example:
int multiply(int, int); // just input ints, pass by value

// suffix is input-only but not as cheap as an int, pass by const&
string& concatenate(string&, const string& suffix);

void sink(unique_ptr<widget>);  // input only, and moves ownership of the widget

Great question! Let's break this down conceptually. A pointer is a variable that holds a memory address—it's like a piece of paper with an address written on it. You can change what address is written, or even erase it (set to nullptr). A reference, on the other hand, is like a nickname for an existing variable—it must be initialized when declared and cannot be changed to refer to another variable later. Think of a pointer as a detachable label, and a reference as a permanent alias. Both allow indirect access, but references are safer and simpler by design.
